answer.summary: Looker accepted a labor-intensive, consulting-like presales tradeoff: Lloyd Tabb spent 20–40 hours with prospects modeling their real data and demonstrating the product before they bought. That hands-on approach let prospects experience Looker’s value directly, and it became repeatable: Looker went from five to 25 customers fairly quickly, with a 75% close rate and zero churn among the customers described.

sections.heading: Tradeoff
sections.content: Because prospects needed to see their own modeled data and dashboards to understand Looker—and mock-ups would not sell it—Tabb worked with them before they became customers. He spent 20, 30, or 40 hours modeling their data, teaching them to use the product, and showing others in the organization what the data and dashboards could reveal. Todd describes the first five customers as essentially receiving consulting, so the tradeoff was substantial founder time and a process more labor-intensive than simply selling a standard product.

sections.heading: What it gained
sections.content: Looker later called this repeatable process its “forward deploy” process; it helped the company figure out sales. After taking a long time to get it right at level one, they moved from five to 25 customers fairly quickly. Todd reports a 75% close rate because they were selling customers who were already using Looker, and zero churn in the account he describes. Tabb said that by 20 customers he knew they were onto something and had figured out a model.
